channel.title: PsyDigest — psychiatry literature digest
channel.description: Summaries of new psychiatric research and guidelines

item.title: [25] Educational Interventions for Perinatal Depression Management Among Non-Specialist Providers in Resource-Constrained Settings: A Descriptive Systematic Review of Limited Evidence.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: A descriptive systematic review examined educational interventions for non-specialist providers managing perinatal depression (PND) in resource-constrained settings, synthesizing quasi-experimental studies published between 2019–2025 across Nigeria, Saudi Arabia, and Thailand.
FINDINGS: Three non-randomized studies (n=351) were included, all judged to be at critical risk of bias using ROBINS-I V2. Educational models commonly used WHO mhGAP frameworks and multi-session, cascade training with mobile supervision, showing improvements in provider-level metrics. No studies assessed patient outcomes, and high attrition and lack of control groups precluded causal inference.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited, methodologically weak, and insufficient to determine whether educational interventions improve PND care or outcomes. The narrative synthesis highlights feasibility and training structure but cannot support clinical recommendations due to critical risk of bias and absence of patient-centered data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings are hypothesis-generating only; routine adoption of these educational models in perinatal depression care is not supported by evidence. High-quality randomized or quasi-experimental trials with patient outcomes are urgently needed before implementation.

item.title: [15] Combining Cognitive Training and Brain Stimulation: A Novel Approach to Address Disordered Eating and Antipsychotic-Induced Weight Gain in People With Severe Mental Illness.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This double-blind, sham-controlled RCT tested whether five sessions of Approach Bias Modification Training (ABMT) combined with real or sham transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) over 3 weeks could reduce food craving and binge eating in adults with schizophrenia/schizoaffective disorder on stable antipsychotics.
FINDINGS: Twenty-eight participants were randomised (93 % of target). Retention was 85.7 % at post-treatment and 78.6 % at 2-week follow-up; blinding accuracy was 46.4 %. Medium effect sizes favoured ABMT + real tDCS for binge eating (d = –0.6, 95 % CI –1.5 to 0.3) and ABMT + sham tDCS for food cravings (d = 0.5, 95 % CI –0.4 to 1.4). Within-group analyses showed reduced approach bias to food and increased avoidance bias only in the real-tDCS arm (all p < 0.05), followed by fewer binge-eating episodes (p < 0.05).
INTERPRETATION: The study demonstrates feasibility and acceptability, with high recruitment and retention, but the small sample and wide confidence intervals mean the apparent medium effects are highly uncertain. The within-group changes suggest a possible synergistic effect of ABMT + real tDCS on approach-avoidance bias, but the absence of a between-group statistical difference precludes firm conclusions. A larger, adequately powered confirmatory trial with stratification by binge-eating disorder diagnosis is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence is insufficient to change practice; the combination may be worth exploring in selected patients, but clinicians should await robust efficacy data before adopting ABMT + tDCS for antipsychotic-induced weight gain.

item.title: [15] Effect of Probiotics on GI Symptom Management in Autism Spectrum Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Clinical Trials.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis examined whether probiotics reduce gastrointestinal (GI) symptoms in individuals with autism spectrum disorder (ASD), a population with high rates of GI comorbidity and proposed gut-brain axis dysfunction. Six clinical trials comparing probiotics (single or multiple strains) to placebo were pooled.
FINDINGS: The overall pooled effect showed a small, non-significant reduction in GI symptoms with probiotics (SMD = −0.189; 95% CI −0.398 to 0.020; p = 0.07; I² = 39.4%). Subgroup analysis suggested single-strain probiotics may modestly improve GI symptoms versus placebo, while multiple-strain formulations did not differ significantly from placebo.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and limited by moderate heterogeneity and a small total sample size. The borderline p-value and small effect size suggest any benefit is likely modest at best. Risk of bias and variability in strains/doses across trials further weaken conclusions. Larger, rigorously designed RCTs with standardized probiotic formulations are needed before clinical recommendations can be made.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not support routine use of probiotics for GI symptoms in ASD. Clinicians should remain cautious about recommending probiotics until higher-quality trials confirm efficacy and define optimal strains/doses.

item.title: [15] Clinical practice guidelines for managing psychosocial difficulties in adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury: considerations for people from culturally and linguistically diverse backgrounds.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This clinical practice guideline addresses how to manage psychosocial difficulties in adults with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury (TBI) from culturally and linguistically diverse (CALD) backgrounds, a group reported to have poorer functional and mental health outcomes. The recommendations were developed using qualitative interviews with CALD individuals with TBI, additional consultations, and integration of existing cultural guidelines in mental health.
FINDINGS: The guideline emphasizes cultural competency training for clinicians, consideration of acculturation levels and migration impacts, culturally sensitive communication (including interpreter use), and understanding psychosocial challenges through a cultural lens. Recommendations are based on qualitative data and expert consultation rather than quantitative outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of this guideline lies in its grounding in qualitative evidence from the target population, highlighting barriers such as stigma, isolation, and communication challenges. However, the lack of quantitative data (e.g., effect sizes, confidence intervals) limits the ability to assess the impact of these recommendations on clinical outcomes. The process involved only a small number of participants and relied heavily on expert consultation, which may introduce bias. External validity is uncertain due to the specific context of CALD individuals with TBI in Australia.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should consider integrating culturally sensitive practices into care plans for CALD patients with TBI, such as using interpreters and assessing acculturation levels. However, the recommendations are based on qualitative insights rather than robust evidence, so their implementation should be monitored for effectiveness in routine care.

item.title: [12] Moving towards evidence-based screening and investigations in first episode psychosis: A commentary on the ANZJP GRADE Schizophrenia Guidelines.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The commentary critiques the ANZJP GRADE Schizophrenia Guidelines, which provide evidence-based recommendations for routine physical health investigations in first episode psychosis (FEP). It highlights gaps in addressing affective psychosis and sexual health screening, emphasizing the need for comprehensive physical health assessment in this population.
FINDINGS: The guidelines prioritize diagnostic clarification and monitoring for iatrogenic harms but may underemphasize sexual health and affective psychosis. The commentary argues that people with FEP represent a high-risk group for sexually transmitted infections (STIs), warranting broader screening than currently recommended.
INTERPRETATION: This is a commentary (not primary research), so it synthesizes existing guidelines rather than presenting new data. Strengths include addressing a critical gap in FEP care, but limitations include lack of quantitative evidence and reliance on expert opinion. The clinical implications depend on whether affective psychosis and STIs are clinically significant in FEP—further research is needed to quantify risks and refine recommendations.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should remain vigilant for sexual health issues and affective psychosis in FEP, even if current guidelines do not mandate routine screening. Further evidence may justify broader investigations in these subgroups.

item.title: [7] Expert guidance to inform coordinated suicide postvention responses: A Delphi study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aimed to establish expert consensus on best practices for implementing Postvention Protocol Response Groups (PPRGs)—coordinated local services supporting communities after a suicide—using a Delphi method with 30 Australian experts (PPRG members, postvention specialists, and bereaved individuals). The clinical question was how to optimally structure PPRGs to enhance their effectiveness and sustainability.
FINDINGS: The Delphi panel endorsed 126 statements (rated ≥80% as "essential" or "important") covering stakeholder engagement, governance, operational practices, data surveillance, and rural-specific considerations. No quantitative effect sizes or statistical tests were reported; the results reflect consensus-based recommendations rather than empirical outcomes.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s strength lies in its structured consensus-building among diverse experts, offering practical guidance for PPRG implementation. However, as a Delphi study, it lacks external validation or measurable outcomes, relying solely on expert opinion. The recommendations are preliminary and may not generalize beyond the Australian context or to non-specialist settings. No clinical significance can be inferred without follow-up studies assessing real-world impact.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This guidance may inform the development of PPRGs in new regions or improve existing programs, but clinicians should await empirical evidence before assuming these practices will improve postvention outcomes. Implementation should be piloted with careful monitoring of feasibility and impact.

item.title: [6] Genome-wide analysis identifies pleiotropic genes shared between severe mental disorders and biomarkers of cellular aging.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This genome-wide association study (GWAS) examined genetic overlap between severe mental disorders (bipolar disorder, major depressive disorder, schizophrenia) and biomarkers of cellular aging (e.g., telomere length, epigenetic age acceleration) to explore whether shared heritability contributes to reduced longevity in these conditions.
FINDINGS: All three disorders showed negative genetic correlation with multivariate longevity/healthy aging (mvAge). Major depressive disorder (MDD) additionally showed negative correlation with leukocyte telomere length (gLTL) and positive correlation with epigenetic age acceleration (gEAA). Nine pleiotropic genes were identified across all disorders and aging biomarkers. Functional analyses implicated increased CRHR1 expression in the prefrontal cortex as potentially increasing risk for MDD and brain age gap (BAG).
INTERPRETATION: This study provides preliminary genetic evidence linking severe mental disorders with cellular aging processes, suggesting shared biological pathways. However, as a GWAS relying on summary-level data, causal inference is limited and effect sizes are not quantified. The findings are hypothesis-generating and require experimental validation. The clinical relevance of identified genes remains uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No immediate change in practice is warranted. These findings may guide future research into mechanisms of accelerated aging in psychiatric disorders and potential therapeutic targets, but translation to patient care is not yet possible.

item.title: [6] HINT1 in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons mediates depressive-like behaviors.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical mouse study examined whether histidine trimeric nucleotide-binding protein 1 (HINT1) in ventral hippocampal GABAergic neurons contributes to depressive-like behaviors after chronic social defeat stress (CSDS), a model of depression-like states in animals.
FINDINGS: Susceptible mice showed ~1.5–2-fold upregulation of HINT1 in hippocampus and mPFC. Targeted vHip HINT1 overexpression increased depressive-like behaviors (e.g., social avoidance p < 0.01, sucrose preference decrease p < 0.05), whereas vHip HINT1 knockdown reversed deficits (effect sizes not reported). The selective HINT1 inhibitor TpGc infused into vHip normalized behavior and neuronal firing. Cell-type work implicated SST+ and PV+ GABAergic neurons; HINT1 overexpression in these subtypes worsened phenotypes. Proteomics linked HINT1 to upregulation of the SUMO E3 ligase CBX4 (~1.8-fold), and CBX4 overexpression in GABAergic vHip neurons induced depressive-like behavior. Mechanistically, HINT1 inhibited PKCβ1 phosphorylation, dampening MEK1/2-ERK1/2 signaling, increasing CBX4, and altering GluN2A SUMOylation and trafficking.
INTERPRETATION: The study uses a robust CSDS paradigm with targeted viral manipulations and pharmacological inhibition, supporting a causal role for HINT1 in vHip GABAergic neurons in depressive-like behaviors. Limitations include lack of effect-size estimates, absence of human data, and reliance on a single stress model in mice. The mechanistic cascade (HINT1→PKCβ1→ERK→CBX4→GluN2A SUMOylation) is plausible but needs replication and translational validation. Overall, the evidence is preliminary but points to HINT1 as a potential upstream regulator warranting further study.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings do not yet change practice; they suggest HINT1 and downstream SUMO pathways as future drug targets. Clinicians should watch for emerging translational studies linking HINT1 biology to human depression before considering any therapeutic implications.

item.title: [6] Substance use disorder, psychiatric illness, and suicide risk among hospitalized incarcerated adults: A retrospective study using National Inpatient Sample (NIS) database.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used a large U.S. claims database (NIS 2016-2021) to examine how substance use disorder (SUD) in hospitalized incarcerated adults is linked to psychiatric comorbidity, suicidality, and hospital outcomes in a retrospective cohort.
FINDINGS: Among 92,715 hospitalized incarcerated adults, 40.4 % had SUD. Suicidal ideation was present in 75.4 % of those with SUD versus 38.6 % without (aOR 3.73, p < .001). SUD was also associated with higher odds of major depressive disorder (aOR 1.43), schizophrenia-spectrum (aOR 1.61), bipolar (aOR 1.66), anxiety (aOR 2.07), trauma-related (aOR 1.90), and personality disorders (aOR 1.63; all p < .001). SUD was linked to lower in-hospital mortality and lower total charges, with no difference in length of stay.
INTERPRETATION: The large sample and clear associations strengthen confidence that SUD co-occurs with severe psychiatric morbidity and suicidality in this population. However, the retrospective design, reliance on ICD-10 codes, and lack of adjustment for unmeasured confounders (e.g., severity of incarceration, prior treatment) limit causal inference. The lower charges and mortality may reflect selection or coding artifacts rather than true clinical benefit. Effect sizes for psychiatric diagnoses are modest despite statistical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Incarcerated inpatients with SUD merit routine, integrated psychiatric screening and suicide risk assessment during hospitalization; current findings do not yet justify specific treatment changes beyond standard dual-diagnosis care.

item.title: [22] Management of shift work disorder: an American Academy of Sleep Medicine clinical practice guideline.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This American Academy of Sleep Medicine (AASM) clinical practice guideline uses a systematic review and GRADE methodology to evaluate treatments for shift work disorder (SWD) in adults, focusing on excessive sleepiness and/or insomnia symptoms. It provides conditional recommendations based on very low to moderate certainty evidence.
FINDINGS: The guideline conditionally recommends modafinil/armodafinil for excessive sleepiness (moderate certainty), bright light therapy (very low certainty), caffeine (very low certainty), clockwise rotating shifts (very low certainty), and pre-shift naps (very low certainty). For insomnia, it conditionally recommends CBT-I (very low certainty), melatonin (very low to low certainty), ramelteon/suvorexant (low certainty), and advises against benzodiazepines (very low certainty). For circadian adaptation, bright light with fixed sleep timing and morning light-blocking glasses are suggested (very low certainty). No preference is given for 8-hour vs. 12-hour night shifts (very low certainty).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is weak (mostly very low certainty), with only modafinil/armodafinil backed by moderate certainty. Recommendations are conditional, emphasizing shared decision-making due to limited high-quality trials. Harms (e.g., sleep inertia with naps/melatonin) and impracticality for rotating shifts are noted. External validity is limited by study populations (often healthy shift workers) and short follow-ups.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Modafinil/armodafinil may modestly help excessive sleepiness in SWD, but other interventions (bright light, caffeine, CBT-I) have uncertain benefits. Clinicians should prioritize sleep hygiene, nap safety, and avoid benzodiazepines for insomnia. Rotating-shift workers may not benefit from circadian adaptation strategies.

item.title: [21] Efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders treated with antipsychotics: a systematic review and meta-analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis of seven RCTs (n=481) assessed the efficacy and safety of GLP-1 receptor agonists (GLP-1 RAs) versus placebo in patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders (SSD) treated with antipsychotics, focusing on weight, metabolic, and psychiatric outcomes.
FINDINGS: GLP-1 RAs significantly reduced body weight (MD -6.98 kg; 95% CI -10.53 to -3.43), BMI (MD -2.51 kg/m²; 95% CI -3.51 to -1.51), waist circumference (MD -5.05 cm; 95% CI -6.66 to -3.44), HbA1c (MD -0.32 percentage points; 95% CI -0.38 to -0.26), and fasting glucose (MD -0.54 mmol/L; 95% CI -0.83 to -0.25). Psychiatric symptoms did not differ between groups (SMD -0.05; 95% CI -0.36 to 0.25). Gastrointestinal adverse events were more frequent with GLP-1 RAs, but overall dropout rates were similar. Heterogeneity was substantial for weight-related outcomes (I² up to 93%).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence suggests GLP-1 RAs improve short-term metabolic parameters in SSD patients, but the high heterogeneity, small sample size, and lack of long-term data limit confidence. The absence of psychiatric symptom improvement suggests the benefits are primarily metabolic. Further large-scale, longer-duration RCTs are needed to confirm efficacy, safety, and generalisability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: GLP-1 RAs may be considered for managing antipsychotic-induced weight gain/metabolic dysfunction in SSD, but clinicians should monitor for gastrointestinal side effects and await more robust evidence before widespread adoption.

item.title: [20] Adjunctive Atypical Antipsychotics in Major Depressive Disorder: A Network Meta-Analysis Perspective and Consensus Panel Discussion.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This expert consensus panel synthesised comparative evidence from two recent network meta-analyses (NMAs) on FDA-approved atypical antipsychotics as adjuncts for adults with major depressive disorder (MDD) and inadequate antidepressant response, aiming to guide clinical decision-making.
FINDINGS: The panel discussed two NMAs that evaluated efficacy, acceptability, and safety of adjunctive atypical antipsychotics in MDD. While the NMAs used different inclusion criteria, treatment-node definitions, and analytical approaches, their comparative findings were broadly concordant. The panel highlighted the need to integrate efficacy with tolerability, patient preferences, and practical considerations when selecting treatments, and recommended earlier consideration of effective adjunctive options when appropriate.
INTERPRETATION: The strength of this consensus lies in the expert synthesis of comparative NMA data, providing a broad overview of relative efficacy and safety. However, the evidence base is indirect (network meta-analytic), and the panel’s conclusions are based on limited methodological detail provided in the abstract. Important limitations include heterogeneity in NMA approaches, lack of head-to-head trials, and limited long-term or phenotype-specific data. The clinical applicability depends heavily on individual patient profiles and local formulary availability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This consensus supports considering FDA-approved atypical antipsychotics as adjunctive therapy in MDD when antidepressants are insufficient, but does not endorse any specific agent. Clinicians should weigh efficacy against side-effect profiles and patient preferences, and remain cautious due to the lack of direct comparative evidence and long-term safety data.

item.title: [20] Efficacy of Non-Invasive Brain Stimulation on the Treatment of Late Life Depression: A Systematic Review and Network Meta-Analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and network meta-analysis (NMA) evaluated the comparative efficacy of non-invasive brain stimulation (NIBS) interventions for late-life depression (LLD) in adults aged ≥60 years, addressing a gap in evidence for this population through randomized controlled trials (RCTs).
FINDINGS: Twenty-five RCTs (n=1344) comparing 15 NIBS modalities were included. Bilateral electroconvulsive therapy (BL-ECT; SMD=1.13, 95% CI 0.37–1.90) and high-frequency rTMS over the left dorsolateral prefrontal cortex (rTMS-10Hz-F3; SMD=0.42, 95% CI 0.02–0.81) showed statistically significant superiority over sham for depressive symptom reduction. Both interventions retained moderate-certainty evidence despite detected inconsistency in the symptom severity network.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate in certainty and derived from RCTs, but the network meta-analytic approach introduces assumptions about indirect comparisons and loop consistency. BL-ECT shows a large effect size but is invasive and typically reserved for severe/refractory cases; rTMS-10Hz-F3 shows a smaller but clinically plausible effect. Other modalities ranked highly lacked robust data, limiting firm conclusions. The detected inconsistency warrants cautious interpretation of comparative rankings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: BL-ECT and high-frequency left-dorsolateral prefrontal rTMS remain the most evidence-supported NIBS options for LLD, though BL-ECT is generally reserved for severe or treatment-resistant depression. Clinicians should prioritize these modalities in appropriate candidates, while recognizing that evidence for other NIBS techniques remains preliminary.

item.title: [15] Psychoeducation for posttraumatic stress disorder in adults: a systematic review of formats and delivery approaches.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined randomized controlled trials (RCTs) assessing the efficacy of psychoeducation—delivered alone or as a primary component—for adults with posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD), aiming to identify effective formats and delivery approaches.
FINDINGS: Twenty-six RCTs (n=3,304) were included. Nine trials reported significant reductions in PTSD symptoms attributable to psychoeducation, with all positive trials using digital delivery and most including some form of human guidance. Effects were inconsistent across studies, and several positive trials showed concerns or high risk of bias. Additional benefits were seen in perceived stress, anxiety, stigma, and help-seeking intentions.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by heterogeneity in interventions, inconsistent outcomes, and risk of bias in several trials. While digital psychoeducation with human support shows promise, the overall effect on core PTSD symptoms is modest and inconsistent. The methodological quality and external validity are constrained by unregistered review processes and variable comparator groups.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Psychoeducation should not be used as a stand-alone treatment for PTSD but may serve as a useful first step in stepped-care models to improve engagement and reduce stigma. Clinicians should prioritize evidence-based trauma-focused therapies while considering psychoeducation as an adjunct, especially in digital formats with guided support.

item.title: [14] Treatment interventions for co-occurring opioid use disorder, and sleep disturbances: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review addresses the understudied intersection of opioid use disorder (OUD), sleep disturbances, and co-occurring psychiatric symptoms (depression, anxiety, PTSD) using PRISMA-ScR guidelines. It synthesizes pharmacological and non-pharmacological interventions targeting sleep in adults with OUD or opioid dependence, aiming to clarify treatment gaps and clinical relevance.
FINDINGS: Fifteen studies (n=1,167) were included, primarily adjunctive to opioid substitution or antagonist therapies. Naltrexone-induced insomnia was common but did not significantly worsen mood; lorazepam mitigated insomnia. Non-opioid pharmacotherapies showed mixed results: guanfacine increased insomnia risk but reduced stress/craving; amitriptyline, prazepam, dronabinol, and neurotransmitter-precursor supplements showed potential for sleep/withdrawal improvement.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited (heterogeneous studies, small samples, no RCTs), precluding firm conclusions. Methodological weaknesses (lack of blinding, high dropout, varied comparators) and unclear funding sources reduce internal validity. External validity is constrained by diverse interventions and populations. The clinical significance of observed effects remains uncertain due to inconsistent outcomes and absence of standardized sleep metrics.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings suggest sleep disturbances in OUD warrant attention, but no definitive treatment recommendations can be made. Clinicians should monitor sleep as part of OUD care while awaiting higher-quality evidence. Integrated, patient-centered approaches are justified but require further research to optimize interventions.

item.title: [10] From Hospital to Outpatient Care After Long-Acting Injectable Antipsychotic Initiation in Bipolar Disorder: Nationwide Evidence From Taiwan.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examined whether initiating second-generation long-acting injectable antipsychotics (SGA-LAIs) in patients with bipolar disorder (BD) in Taiwan shifts healthcare utilization from acute to outpatient settings, using nationwide retrospective data. The mirror-image design compared the 12 months before and after SGA-LAI initiation.
FINDINGS: Among 17,513 SGA-LAI initiators, 2,937 had BD, and 500 stable users were analyzed. After initiation, both stable and nonstable users showed increased psychiatric outpatient visits (e.g., +X% in stable users) and expenditures, alongside reduced emergency department (ED) visits (e.g., -Y%) and inpatient admissions (e.g., -Z%). The shift toward ambulatory care was more pronounced in stable users.
INTERPRETATION: The study’s mirror-image design and large nationwide sample strengthen internal validity, but the lack of randomization and reliance on administrative data introduce confounding (e.g., unmeasured clinical severity). The focus on healthcare utilization—not relapse or symptom outcomes—limits conclusions about clinical efficacy. The "stable use" subgroup analysis reflects implementation fidelity rather than drug efficacy. Confidence in the findings is moderate due to potential residual confounding and generalizability limited to Taiwan’s single-payer system.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: SGA-LAI initiation in BD may reduce acute-care reliance and increase outpatient engagement, particularly with sustained use. However, this does not confirm superior efficacy over oral antipsychotics; rather, it suggests better continuity of care with LAIs in this setting. Clinicians should weigh these utilization shifts against costs, patient preferences, and alternatives.

item.title: [10] An Individual Meta-Analysis of Psychological Treatments for Mood and Personality Disorders Using the Severity Diagnostic System of ICD-11.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study used an individual patient meta-analysis of four RCTs (n=1,384) to test whether ICD-11 personality-disorder severity levels (none → personality difficulty → moderate → severe) differentially predict short-term (12–24 m) outcomes after psychological treatments (mostly CBT) versus control conditions for mood/anxiety symptoms and social function.
FINDINGS: Higher ICD-11 severity was linearly associated with worse baseline mood/anxiety symptoms; moderate and severe PD groups showed significantly less improvement in anxiety than the no-PD group (effect sizes not reported). Depressive-symptom change was inconsistent across trials. Social function improved in all groups. Treatment effects were small and did not differ by PD severity.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate in quality (pooled individual-level data from four RCTs, but proxy PD severity measures and no formal severity-by-treatment interaction test). The consistent baseline gradient supports the dimensional ICD-11 PD severity model, but the lack of differential treatment response limits clinical utility. Small effect sizes and heterogeneity in depressive outcomes suggest results are preliminary rather than definitive.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify tailoring psychological treatment intensity by ICD-11 PD severity; standard CBT remains appropriate while further trials with validated PD severity measures are awaited.

item.title: [9] Metabolic biomarker levels before and after initiation of GLP-1 receptor agonist treatment among individuals with schizophrenia: interrupted time-series analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Observational register-based study examining whether initiating GLP-1 receptor agonist (GLP-1RA) treatment in real-world patients with schizophrenia leads to reductions in HbA1c, LDL and triglycerides, addressing the gap between RCT efficacy and routine care effectiveness.
FINDINGS: Among 3042 individuals with schizophrenia initiating GLP-1RA, HbA1c fell by 11.4% (diabetes indication) and 3.4% (overweight indication), LDL by 6.2% and 4.9%, and triglycerides by 14.8% and 12.7%, respectively; all changes were statistically significant (p < 0.001).
INTERPRETATION: Strengths include large nationwide sample and real-world design; however, lack of a comparator group, potential confounding by indication, and absence of data on medication adherence or lifestyle changes limit causal inference. The magnitude of change is modest and may not translate into clinically meaningful cardiovascular risk reduction for all patients.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support considering GLP-1RA for metabolic risk in schizophrenia, but decisions should be individualised and balanced against side-effects and cost; ongoing monitoring of metabolic parameters remains essential.

item.title: [8] Assessing Suicide Risk Reduction in the Interval Before Death by Suicide Using Natural Language Processing.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This exploratory cohort study used natural language processing (NLP) to compare care patterns in the 6 months before suicide among U.S. Veterans Affairs (VA) patients whose high suicide-risk status was removed shortly before death (Reduced Clinical Risk Classification, RCRC, n=89) versus those whose high-risk status persisted (Sustained Clinical Risk Classification, SCRC, n=89).
FINDINGS: RCRC patients were younger and had fewer psychiatric diagnoses. Topic modeling identified psychotherapy-related terms (“Psychotherapy,” “Follow-up”) in RCRC records and medically structured terms (“Medication,” “Outpatient,” “Suicide-Assessment”) in SCRC records. After risk declassification, RCRC patients showed sharp declines across all topics, whereas SCRC patients maintained or increased engagement.
INTERPRETATION: The study is small, retrospective, and VA-specific, limiting generalisability to other settings. NLP-derived lexical patterns suggest contrasting care trajectories, but causality cannot be inferred. The observed dichotomy may reflect perceived improvement leading to reduced surveillance rather than true risk reduction. Larger, prospective studies with clinician-rated outcomes are needed to validate these findings and assess clinical significance.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not justify changing practice; clinicians should remain vigilant for subtle risk changes even when structured risk assessments suggest improvement.

item.title: [7] Polygenicity shapes distinct brain patterns and clinical profiles of bipolar disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This multi-cohort, multi-ancestry genetic-neuroimaging study asks whether polygenic risk for bipolar disorder (BD) in East Asian populations maps onto specific brain imaging-derived phenotypes (IDPs) and whether these genetic-brain links carry clinical meaning. It integrates individual-level and summary-level data from >10 000 participants to perform cross-trait meta-analysis, fine-mapping, Mendelian randomisation and phenome-wide analyses.
FINDINGS: Eleven pleiotropic SNVs were identified across BD-IDP pairs, enriched for lipid metabolism and neurotransmitter pathways. An East-Asian-specific signal (rs7941324 near RPS27P20) showed high posterior inclusion probability only in EAS. Bidirectional Mendelian randomisation implicated 27 IDP→BD and 35 BD→IDP causal relationships; parietal/temporal gyri changes appeared pre-onset while right precuneus change tracked disease state. Polygenic risk scores combining BD-IDP signals correlated with depressive and anxiety symptom burden and with suicide risk (mediated by these symptoms). PRS-PheWAS linked the same score to 135 metabolic traits.
INTERPRETATION: The study leverages large, ancestrally diverse datasets and triangulates genetic, imaging and clinical data with several causal inference methods, strengthening internal validity. However, effect sizes for individual loci are modest and the PRS explains only a small fraction of variance in clinical outcomes; thus statistical significance does not yet translate into clinically actionable prediction. Population specificity (EAS-only discovery) limits immediate generalisability to European or other ancestries. The mediation findings are observational and cannot establish causality.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, these results do not change bedside practice; they highlight potential mechanistic pathways (lipid/neurotransmitter biology, parietal-temporal cortex development) and risk domains (mood symptoms, suicidality, metabolic comorbidity) that may inform future stratified or preventative strategies rather than guide current treatment choices.

item.title: [7] Jail-based opioid treatment implementation, outcomes, and costs: lessons learned from the Massachusetts Justice Community Opioid Innovation Network (MassJCOIN).
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study examines the implementation, outcomes, and costs of jail-based medications for opioid use disorder (MOUD) in Massachusetts, where a legislative mandate required pilot jails to offer all FDA-approved MOUDs, ensure continuity upon release, and facilitate community continuation. It is a Type 1 hybrid effectiveness-implementation study conducted within the Massachusetts Justice Community Opioid Innovation Network (MassJCOIN), focusing on incarcerated individuals with opioid use disorder.
FINDINGS: The program improved treatment engagement and reduced recidivism, with implementation facilitators including universal MOUD access policies, adaptive leadership, adequate staffing, diversion prevention, and consideration of patient preferences and co-occurring mental health conditions. Post-release continuity was supported by re-entry planning and community treatment system alignment. Site-specific cost data were provided to inform program design and resource allocation. The legislative mandate and statewide system changes were identified as key drivers of success.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and descriptive, drawing on selected MassJCOIN findings rather than a single rigorous trial. The study lacks a control group, effect sizes, or statistical comparisons, limiting causal inference. While the program appears feasible and beneficial within a harm reduction framework, generalisability depends on the unique Massachusetts policy and community treatment context. The cost data are informative but not generalisable without further economic evaluation.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support the clinical and public health value of jail-based MOUD programs, particularly when paired with robust re-entry planning. Clinicians should advocate for such programs in carceral settings, ensuring continuity of care and addressing co-occurring mental health needs. However, implementation should be tailored to local resources and policy environments, and further research is needed to quantify clinical and economic outcomes.

item.title: [6] Total cost of care for long-acting injectable antipsychotics for schizophrenia: Pharmacy vs medical benefit.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared total cost of care (TCOC) and healthcare resource utilisation (HCRU) among commercially insured US patients with schizophrenia receiving long-acting injectable antipsychotics (LAIs) under pharmacy vs medical benefit. A retrospective cohort design was used to address payer coverage differences, a clinically relevant but under-studied question.
FINDINGS: After propensity score matching (n=61 per cohort), mean direct-cause medical TCOC was $7,569 higher in the medical-benefit cohort (P=0.023). When LAI drug spend was included, total spend favoured the pharmacy-benefit cohort by $3,673, but this difference was not statistically significant (P=0.34). The medical-benefit cohort had higher all-cause inpatient costs (+$12,633; P=0.01), all-cause total medical costs (+$18,582; P=0.02), and 8.90 more inpatient claims per member (P=0.006). No significant differences were found in pharmacy benefit costs (excluding LAI), ED utilisation, outpatient costs/utilisation, or total utilisation.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is moderate-strength due to the retrospective design, small matched sample, and reliance on administrative claims data. The large inpatient cost differential suggests that administrative billing pathway may influence utilisation, but residual confounding (e.g., unmeasured illness severity) cannot be excluded. The lack of difference in total spend after including LAI drug cost implies that payer coverage model alone may not drive overall expenditure. Findings should be replicated in larger, clinically enriched cohorts with longer follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence does not mandate a change in prescribing practice based solely on billing pathway. Clinicians should remain alert to potential administrative drivers of hospitalisation and discuss coverage options with patients and payers, but prioritise clinical appropriateness of LAI choice over cost-minimisation strategy.

item.title: [6] Ketamine Modulates Endogenous Opioid Peptide Signaling and Reduces Heroin-Seeking in Male Long-Evans Rats.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study in male Long-Evans rats examined whether ketamine modulates endogenous opioid signaling and reduces heroin-seeking behavior, addressing the urgent need for novel treatments for Opioid Use Disorder (OUD). The study used molecular, protein, and behavioral assays to explore mechanisms and outcomes.
FINDINGS: Molecular analyses showed increased expression of endogenous opioid system genes and peptides, elevated mu-opioid receptor protein levels, and enhanced G protein activity, particularly in the nucleus accumbens shell. Ketamine also altered NMDAR subunit expression in the medial prefrontal cortex and nucleus accumbens. Behaviorally, ketamine significantly reduced heroin-primed (but not cue-induced) seeking in a self-administration paradigm.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed animal study with mechanistic depth, but its external validity is limited by species and sex (male rats only). The behavioral effect is specific to heroin-primed relapse, not cue-induced relapse, which may not fully capture human OUD complexity. The clinical relevance of these molecular changes remains uncertain without human data. The study suggests potential therapeutic mechanisms but requires replication and translation to clinical settings.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings are preliminary and do not yet justify changes in clinical practice for OUD. Further research—especially in humans—is needed to determine whether ketamine’s opioid-modulating effects translate into meaningful reductions in relapse risk.

item.title: [29] Digital Therapeutic Interventions for Suicide Prevention: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Their Effectiveness in Reducing Suicidal Ideation and Suicide Attempts.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses whether digital therapeutic interventions (e.g., apps, online programs) reduce suicidal ideation or suicide attempts in randomized clinical trials (RCTs). It synthesizes 17 RCTs (N = 5,089) to clarify mixed prior findings and assess durability of effects.
FINDINGS: Digital interventions significantly reduced suicidal ideation immediately (Hedges’ g = –0.61, 95 % CI not reported) and at follow-up (g = –0.77). The relative risk of suicide attempts was reduced (RR ≈ 0.7–0.8) but not statistically significant. Effects were larger in clinical populations, self-guided formats, and younger participants; heterogeneity was high (I² not reported).
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is moderate-sized but heterogeneous, with potential risk of bias across diverse digital formats and control conditions. The statistically significant reduction in suicidal ideation is of uncertain clinical magnitude; the non-significant trend for fewer attempts precludes firm conclusions. Publication bias assessment was limited and funding sources were not disclosed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Digital interventions may offer a useful adjunct for reducing suicidal thoughts, especially in younger or clinical subgroups, but current evidence does not yet justify replacing standard care for suicide prevention. Clinicians should monitor emerging high-quality RCTs before integrating these tools routinely.

item.title: [15] Learning from neurodivergent students about their mental health and wellbeing during transition to secondary school: A systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study addresses how the transition from primary to secondary school affects mental health and wellbeing in neurodivergent children (e.g., autistic youth, those with developmental language disorder, or Down syndrome), using a neurodiversity-informed framework. It is a systematic review of longitudinal empirical studies with child-reported outcomes, aiming to clarify inconsistent findings in this emerging research area.
FINDINGS: Out of 488 records screened, only 10 studies met inclusion criteria, all longitudinal with comparison groups and at least two timepoints around the school transition. Due to substantial heterogeneity, a narrative synthesis was conducted. Findings on mental health outcomes were mixed and inconclusive, but psychosocial factors—such as school belonging and connectedness—showed more consistent vulnerability signals. Key gaps included lack of participatory research, underrepresentation of certain neurodivergent groups, and limited attention to intersectional factors like ethnicity and socioeconomic status.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is very limited and heterogeneous, with no meta-analysis possible. The reliance on narrative synthesis and small, varied samples reduces confidence in any firm conclusions. The stronger signal in psychosocial outcomes suggests these may be more sensitive indicators than mental health symptoms, but causality and clinical significance remain unclear. The absence of co-produced research and intersectional analyses limits generalisability and clinical applicability.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current findings do not support specific clinical recommendations for managing mental health during school transition in neurodivergent youth. Clinicians should prioritise monitoring psychosocial adjustment (e.g., belonging, school concerns) rather than assuming uniform mental health deterioration. Future practice should await more rigorous, participatory, and intersectionally informed research before implementing targeted interventions.

item.title: [12] Metabolic syndrome in stable long-term antipsychotic monotherapy and polypharmacy among patients with schizophrenia: a real-world comparative study.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This retrospective cohort study in a Swedish community mental health centre asked whether antipsychotic polypharmacy, compared with monotherapy, is independently associated with metabolic syndrome in adults with schizophrenia who had been on a stable regimen for ≥5 years. 370 patients were included.
FINDINGS: Metabolic syndrome was present in 38.6 % overall (41.2 % polypharmacy vs 34.7 % monotherapy, p = 0.216). Polypharmacy patients had higher chlorpromazine-equivalent doses (median 1010 vs 454.5 mg/day, p < 0.001) and more LAI use (67.3 % vs 37.5 %, p < 0.001). In multivariable logistic regression, neither polypharmacy (adjusted OR 1.220, 95 % CI 0.767–1.941, p = 0.401), daily dose increments of 100 mg (adjusted OR 1.003, 95 % CI 0.954–1.055, p = 0.899), nor LAI use were independently linked to metabolic syndrome. Current smoking showed the only independent association (adjusted OR 1.996, 95 % CI 1.251–3.185, p = 0.004).
INTERPRETATION: The study’s retrospective design and selection of long-term stable patients limit causal inference; residual confounding (e.g., illness severity, prior treatments) cannot be excluded. The confidence intervals around the null associations are wide, so clinically meaningful effects cannot be ruled out. The clearest modifiable risk factor was smoking, underscoring the need for cardiometabolic monitoring and smoking cessation interventions regardless of regimen.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: For patients on long-term antipsychotic treatment, switching from polypharmacy to monotherapy primarily to reduce metabolic risk is not supported by these data. Focus should remain on routine metabolic screening and smoking cessation rather than regimen simplification per se.

item.title: [11] Peripartum Esketamine: A Narrative Review of Analgesia, Postpartum Depressive Symptoms, Sleep-Related Outcomes, and Safety.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review examines whether peripartum esketamine can improve pain control, reduce postpartum depressive symptoms, enhance sleep, and maintain maternal-infant safety. It synthesizes mechanistic rationale and clinical studies, primarily single-center trials in cesarean-delivery populations.
FINDINGS: Short-term analgesic benefit is consistently reported, but opioid-sparing effects are inconsistent. Several RCTs suggest low-dose peri-delivery esketamine may lower early Edinburgh Postnatal Depression Scale (EPDS) screening positives, though diagnostic outcomes are sparse. Sleep benefits are preliminary and based on subjective measures. Maternal and neonatal tolerability appear acceptable in the short term, but pregnancy pharmacokinetics, lactation data, and long-term offspring neurodevelopment remain insufficiently studied.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by study design heterogeneity, small single-center samples, and reliance on screening tools rather than diagnostic interviews. Strengths include consistent short-term analgesic findings and signals for mood improvement, but the lack of objective sleep measures, standardized dosing, and long-term safety data constrains confidence. The clinical significance of observed mood effects is uncertain given the absence of diagnostic confirmation and long-term follow-up.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Esketamine may be considered as an individualized adjunct for peripartum pain management, but routine prophylactic use for mood or sleep is not supported by current evidence. Clinicians should await larger multicenter trials with diagnostic outcomes and long-term safety assessments before changing practice.

item.title: [10] Feasibility and Acceptability of Videoconference-Based Family Psychoeducation for Young Adult Caregivers of Family Members With Major Depressive Disorder: Protocol for a Pilot Randomized Controlled Trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This is a protocol for a waitlist-controlled pilot randomized controlled trial (RCT) examining the feasibility and acceptability of videoconference-based family psychoeducation (vFPE) for young adult caregivers (aged 18–39) of family members with major depressive disorder (MDD). The study addresses a gap in support programs for this vulnerable group, who face psychological distress and caregiving burdens during a critical developmental period.
FINDINGS: The protocol outlines a 1:1 randomized trial with 4 weekly 40-minute vFPE sessions. Primary outcomes are feasibility (recruitment, randomization, completion, dropout, safety) and acceptability (Client Satisfaction Questionnaire-8). Exploratory outcomes (e.g., anxiety, depression, caregiver burden) will be assessed at baseline, postintervention, and 1-month follow-up. As of May 2026, 8 participants had been enrolled, with recruitment and data collection ongoing until March 2028.
INTERPRETATION: This is a feasibility study, not designed to test efficacy. Strengths include its randomized design and focus on a neglected population, but conclusions are premature given the small sample size and ongoing recruitment. The protocol’s rigor depends on adherence to randomization and blinding (if any), but no effect sizes or preliminary results are yet available. External validity is uncertain until feasibility metrics (e.g., dropout rates, satisfaction) are reported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No clinical conclusions can be drawn yet. If feasibility is demonstrated, this could pave the way for a larger RCT to assess effectiveness. Clinicians should monitor future results to determine whether vFPE is a viable option for young adult caregivers in routine care.

item.title: [10] A Typology of Moderator Practices and Community Guidelines in Online Mental Health Communities to Establish a Framework for Digital Safety: Systematized Review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Online mental health communities (OMHCs) provide peer support but face challenges in ensuring safety and supportive interactions through moderation practices and community guidelines. This systematized review aimed to develop typologies of moderator practices and guideline content in OMHCs for people with mental health problems, synthesizing empirical and gray literature from 2014 to 2024.
FINDINGS: The review included 80 documents (48 empirical papers and 32 gray literature) covering 52 OMHCs. Four categories of moderator practices were identified: (1) premoderation/postmoderation processes (used in 79% of OMHCs), (2) reactive moderation, (3) community-building, and (4) member monitoring. Three categories of community guideline content emerged: (1) content of posts (used in 67% of OMHCs), (2) member conduct, and (3) moderation. Thematic analysis synthesized these findings into a structured framework.
INTERPRETATION: This systematized review provides a structured framework for moderator practices and guideline content in OMHCs, addressing a critical gap in digital safety. Strengths include the broad inclusion of empirical and gray literature and the development of actionable typologies. However, as a systematized review (not a full systematic review), it lacks formal risk-of-bias assessment and may overrepresent certain OMHCs. The findings are descriptive and lack quantitative effect sizes or comparative data. External validity depends on the diversity of OMHCs included, which may not fully represent all platforms or cultural contexts.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This framework could guide the development of moderator training, digital tools, and governance policies in OMHCs, potentially improving safety and support for users. Clinicians should be aware of these typologies when recommending or evaluating OMHCs, but further research is needed to assess their impact on user outcomes and safety.

item.title: [9] Altered GABAB receptor sensitivity in heavy drinkers indexed using a TMS-based biomarker: a randomized controlled experimental medicine trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study tested whether heavy alcohol use alters sensitivity of metabotropic GABAB receptors (GABABRs) using transcranial magnetic stimulation (TMS) biomarkers and a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover design in 31 healthy volunteers (16 heavy drinkers, 15 light drinkers).
FINDINGS: Baclofen 30 mg and 60 mg produced dose-dependent increases in growth hormone (GH) release, confirming central GABABR engagement. Long-interval intracortical inhibition (LICI) increased after baclofen in light drinkers at both doses, suggesting a plateau effect. In heavy drinkers, LICI increased at 30 mg but not at 60 mg despite similar drug levels, indicating altered GABABR sensitivity under higher agonist stimulation.
INTERPRETATION: The randomized crossover design and biomarker confirmation strengthen internal validity. The small sample and healthy volunteer population limit generalizability to clinical AUD. The differential LICI response at higher dose suggests altered receptor function in heavy drinkers, but clinical significance remains uncertain without outcome data.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Findings support further investigation of TMS-based biomarkers for GABABR target engagement but do not yet justify changes in AUD treatment. Watch for emerging studies linking these biomarkers to clinical outcomes.

item.title: [9] Exercise as a complementary intervention for adults with attention deficit hyperactivity disorder: a neurobiological analysis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This narrative review explores potential neurobiological mechanisms by which physical exercise could alleviate symptoms of inattention, hyperactivity, and impulsivity in adults with ADHD, where evidence for exercise as a treatment is limited compared to children.
FINDINGS: The review synthesizes mechanistic hypotheses—including enhanced neuroplasticity, improved functional brain connectivity, neurotransmitter modulation, and reduced neuroinflammation—based on heterogeneous, largely observational data and indirect evidence from non-ADHD populations. No clinical outcome data or effect sizes are reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and methodologically weak: reliance on a single database, single-author screening, and lack of direct adult ADHD intervention studies limit internal validity. The proposed mechanisms are biologically plausible but remain unconfirmed in the target population. External validity is uncertain due to indirect data sources.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Exercise may hold promise as a low-cost, accessible adjunct for adults with ADHD, but current evidence is insufficient to recommend it as a treatment. Clinicians should view exercise as supportive care while awaiting rigorous trials to confirm efficacy and clarify mechanisms.

item.title: [9] Design, reporting, and research focus of neurology and psychiatry drug trials (2020-2023): a registry-based meta-epidemiological study using ClinicalTrials.gov and NLP.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This registry-based meta-epidemiological study used ClinicalTrials.gov data (2000–2023) with NLP and manual validation to quantify design features, reporting practices, and research focus in neurology and psychiatry drug trials. The clinical question concerns how these trials are conducted and reported, which affects evidence synthesis and future trial planning.
FINDINGS: Among 18,609 trials, most were early-phase (60% completed), single-center, and small (median 11–50 participants). Industry funded 36%, declining over time; university sponsorship increased. Ten percent were non-randomized and 38% open-label. Among trials completed after 2007, only 50% reported results, with a mean delay of 12 months. Top conditions studied were pain (10%), schizophrenia (8%), depression (8%), and Alzheimer’s disease (7%). Atypical antipsychotics, levodopa, and ketamine each accounted for 1–2% of trials.
INTERPRETATION: The study highlights persistent deficiencies in trial design (small size, high proportion of non-randomized/open-label trials) and poor results reporting (only half reported results, often delayed). While the large sample size and use of NLP strengthen internal validity, reliance on registry data and lack of clinical outcome assessment limit external validity. The findings suggest a need for improved adherence to reporting standards and better trial design to enhance evidence quality.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should be cautious when interpreting underpowered, open-label, or industry-funded trials in neurology and psychiatry. Improved trial registration and results reporting are essential for evidence-based practice.

item.title: [7] Extended reality as an assistive technology for mental health and wellbeing: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This scoping review asks whether Extended Reality (XR—virtual, augmented, and mixed reality) can meaningfully advance mental-health care across conditions such as anxiety, depression, PTSD, ADHD, and autism, given persistent barriers to conventional treatments. Using PRISMA-ScR methods, 277 empirical studies published January 2022–March 2025 were synthesised thematically.
FINDINGS: XR applications spanned anxiety/stress (most frequently studied), depression/mood disorders, PTSD, neurodevelopmental conditions, social isolation, cognitive decline, and workplace stress. Reported benefits were predominantly short-term or preliminary, especially for anxiety and PTSD. Design approaches included immersive exposure, mindfulness/relaxation, social interaction, cognitive stimulation, biofeedback, haptics, and adaptive personalisation. Key constraints were limited longitudinal and comparative evidence, high costs, accessibility barriers, clinician training needs, and ethical/privacy/regulatory concerns.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is preliminary and heterogeneous; most studies are small, short-term, and lack robust comparators. While XR shows promise—particularly for anxiety and PTSD—there is insufficient high-quality evidence to establish sustained clinical impact or cost-effectiveness. Stronger randomised trials with longer follow-up, pragmatic comparisons to usual care, and attention to equity, training, and regulation are needed before widespread adoption.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: At present, XR should be considered experimental for routine psychiatric care; clinicians may cautiously explore XR tools in anxiety/PTSD within research or highly supervised settings, but should not yet adopt them as standard interventions.

item.title: [21] Bipolar Disorder and the Risk of Cardiovascular Diseases: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Observational Studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review and meta-analysis (PROSPERO registered) quantified the prevalence and incidence of cardiovascular diseases (CVD) in adults with bipolar disorder (BD) using observational studies, addressing a key gap in understanding premature mortality risk in this population.
FINDINGS: The pooled CVD prevalence in BD was 7.70% (95% CI: 5.07–11.52), with coronary artery disease at 6.89% (95% CI: 4.05–11.47), cerebrovascular disease at 4.45% (95% CI: 2.13–9.05), and peripheral arterial disease at 3.30% (95% CI: 1.66–6.45). In controlled incidence studies, BD was associated with a 66% higher CVD incidence (IRR 1.66, 95% CI: 1.32–2.08), including elevated risks for coronary and cerebrovascular events.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is limited by extreme heterogeneity in prevalence estimates, reliance on observational designs, and insufficient data on moderators (e.g., medication, lifestyle, comorbidities). While the increased CVD incidence in BD is statistically robust, the pooled estimates are imprecise and not generalizable to specific populations. The lack of adjustment for confounders and noncomparable reporting further weakens causal inference.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: The findings support routine cardiovascular screening in adults with BD, but the magnitude and drivers of risk remain uncertain. Clinicians should monitor cardiometabolic health closely, but should not assume precise risk estimates based on these pooled data. Further prospective studies with standardized reporting are needed.

item.title: [19] Efficacy and safety of non-hormonal pharmacotherapies for depressive and anxiety symptoms during the menopausal transition and postmenopause: a systematic review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined the efficacy and safety of non-hormonal drugs (SSRIs, SNRIs, gabapentinoids, etc.) for depressive and anxiety symptoms in peri- and postmenopausal women, synthesizing heterogeneous randomized and non-randomized studies.
FINDINGS: Thirty-one studies (n = 8,124) were included. SNRIs showed more frequent positive effects on depressive symptoms than other classes, while SSRIs had modest and variable effects. Gabapentinoids improved vasomotor symptoms but had limited, low-certainty effects on mood. Anxiety outcomes were inconsistent across all classes. Overall certainty of evidence was very low to moderate.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by clinical and methodological heterogeneity, indirect comparisons, and lack of head-to-head trials, reducing confidence in conclusions. SNRIs may offer the most consistent benefit for depressive symptoms, but effect sizes and certainty remain uncertain. Anxiety outcomes remain insufficiently supported.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Current evidence supports cautious consideration of SNRIs for depressive symptoms in menopausal women, but high-quality comparative trials are needed before firm treatment recommendations can be made.

item.title: [17] Implementation strategies used in clinical practice guidelines in older adults' mental health and neurocognitive conditions: a scoping review.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clinical practice guidelines (CPGs) aim to improve care for older adults with mental health and neurocognitive conditions, but their implementation in practice remains challenging. This scoping review systematically mapped evidence on implementation strategies for CPGs in this population using the JBI methods and EPOC framework.
FINDINGS: Only three peer-reviewed studies were identified. Reported strategies included provider-tailored education and interdisciplinary collaboration. Barriers to implementation included lengthy CPGs, weak evidence perception, and provider doubts about patient relevance. The review highlights a significant gap in the literature.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is extremely limited (n=3 studies), precluding robust conclusions. The review’s strength lies in its systematic mapping, but the paucity of studies and lack of quantitative outcomes undermine internal validity. External validity is unclear due to heterogeneity and unclear generalisability. The findings are preliminary and highlight a critical research gap rather than actionable evidence.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: No direct clinical recommendations can be made from this review. It underscores the need for rigorous studies evaluating effective implementation strategies for CPGs in older adult mental health care. Clinicians should remain cautious about relying on untested strategies.

item.title: [10] Association between clozapine-induced hypertriglyceridemia and defenestration of liver sinusoidal endothelial cells.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Clozapine is the most effective antipsychotic but causes severe metabolic side effects, possibly via liver sinusoidal endothelial cell (LSEC) dysfunction. This translational study combined in vitro murine LSEC porosity assays with human serum analyses to test whether clozapine exposure reduces LSEC porosity and correlates with hypertriglyceridemia and hyperglycemia.
FINDINGS: In 72 routine blood samples from clozapine-treated patients, serum clozapine concentration correlated with triglycerides (Spearman’s ρ = 0.47, P = 0.00024) and glucose (ρ = 0.24, P = 0.034), but not with LDL (ρ = –0.04, P = 0.82) or HDL (ρ = –0.22, P = 0.088). In vitro, clozapine caused a concentration-dependent reduction in murine LSEC porosity (P for trend = 0.00036).
INTERPRETATION: The study provides preliminary mechanistic and correlational evidence linking clozapine to LSEC defenestration and metabolic derangements. The human data are observational and cross-sectional, so causality cannot be inferred. The in vitro findings are robust but in a non-human system. Effect sizes are moderate for triglycerides and small for glucose; clinical significance remains uncertain until prospective human data confirm whether LSEC changes precede or merely reflect metabolic disturbances.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: These findings suggest a potential therapeutic target (LSEC porosity) to mitigate clozapine’s metabolic toxicity, but they do not yet change routine monitoring or clozapine prescribing practices. Watch for future interventional studies targeting LSEC function in clozapine-treated patients.

item.title: [6] Two distinct projection pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons to contribute to fear memory retrieval.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This preclinical study in mice examined whether projection pathways from the postrhinal cortex (POR) to the basolateral amygdala (BLA) contribute to context-induced fear memory retrieval, alongside previously identified ventral hippocampus CA1 (vCA1)-BLA projections. The work aims to clarify neural circuit mechanisms relevant to PTSD relapse prevention.
FINDINGS: The authors report that optogenetic manipulation of POR-BLA neurons modulates context-induced fear memory retrieval in mice. They further show that both POR-BLA and vCA1-BLA pathways converge onto the same BLA neurons, suggesting coordinated involvement in fear memory expression. No quantitative effect sizes, confidence intervals, or p-values are provided in the abstract.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence is preliminary and based on animal neurocircuitry research with limited methodological detail in the abstract. While the convergence of two distinct pathways onto common BLA neurons is a plausible mechanism for fear memory retrieval, the clinical relevance remains uncertain. The study lacks human data, effect sizes, and statistical reporting, so the strength of the conclusion cannot be assessed. Further replication and translational studies are needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study does not yet change clinical practice. It offers a mechanistic hypothesis about fear memory circuits that may guide future translational research, but direct implications for PTSD treatment or patient care are not established.

item.title: [6] Network localization of brain structural and functional alterations induced by electroconvulsive therapy for depression.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study aimed to clarify how electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) alters brain structure and function in depression by synthesizing neuroimaging findings and mapping them onto large-scale brain networks. It combined data from 34 published studies (15 structural and 19 functional MRI studies) with connectome datasets to identify ECT-modulated networks.
FINDINGS: The analysis identified distinct ECT-modulated structural and functional networks. The structural network primarily involved subcortical regions (hippocampus, amygdala), ventral attention areas (insula, operculum, temporoparietal junction), and somatomotor regions (precentral and postcentral gyrus). The functional network mainly implicated the default mode network (medial prefrontal cortex, posterior cingulate cortex).
INTERPRETATION: This is a meta-analytic and network-mapping study, not a primary clinical trial, so causal inferences about ECT’s antidepressant effects cannot be drawn. The strength lies in integrating heterogeneous neuroimaging data to propose a network-level mechanism, but the clinical relevance of these structural/functional changes remains uncertain. The dissociation between structural and functional networks is intriguing but preliminary; replication in larger, longitudinal cohorts with clinical outcome data is needed.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: This study suggests ECT may exert its antidepressant effects through network-specific brain changes, but it does not yet inform treatment decisions. Clinicians should note that ECT’s mechanisms likely involve distributed brain networks rather than isolated regions, but this remains a research finding until linked to patient outcomes.

item.title: [19] Acceptability and Experience of Cognitive Behavioural Therapy for Adult ADHD: A Systematic Review With Narrative Synthesis.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review with narrative synthesis examined the acceptability of cognitive behavioural therapy (CBT) for adults with ADHD, addressing a gap in understanding how core ADHD symptoms may influence treatment engagement and satisfaction. The review included 21 studies (RCTs, pilot/feasibility trials, qualitative and mixed-methods studies) and mapped findings to the seven domains of the Theoretical Framework of Acceptability (TFA).
FINDINGS: Acceptability was most consistently assessed in the domains of affective attitude, intervention coherence, perceived effectiveness, and self-efficacy. Positive drivers included skills training, psychoeducation, therapeutic support, accountability strategies, and individualisation. Burden was primarily associated with homework demands, cognitive load, and treatment intensity. Group and digital formats were generally acceptable but depended on facilitation quality, accessibility, and therapeutic presence. Ethicality and opportunity costs were rarely reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is heterogeneous, combining diverse study designs and measures, which limits firm conclusions. However, the synthesis suggests that CBT for adult ADHD is most acceptable when it enhances engagement, understanding, and perceived benefit while minimising burden. The review highlights the importance of intervention content and delivery style over format alone. Key limitations include the lack of standardised acceptability measures and underreporting of ethical and opportunity-cost domains.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritise structured, flexible CBT interventions that incorporate psychoeducation, skills training, and accountability strategies to improve acceptability. Attention to homework load and cognitive demands may reduce treatment burden. Further research using standardised acceptability measures is needed to refine delivery approaches.

item.title: [16] Outcomes of Mindful Mood Balance for Moms, online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy for perinatal depressive relapse prevention in the USA: a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic randomised clinical trial.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study evaluated whether adding an online mindfulness-based cognitive therapy programme (Mindful Mood Balance for Moms) to usual care reduces depressive relapse and symptom burden in euthymic pregnant women with recurrent depression in the USA, using a two-arm, single-blind, pragmatic RCT.
FINDINGS: In 500 participants (mean age 32 years, mean 11.5 weeks gestation), MMB for Moms reduced relapse risk over 6 months postpartum (33% vs 44%; hazard ratio 0.74, 95% CI 0.56–0.99; p=0.045). Symptom burden decreased more during the 12-week intervention (average PHQ-9 reduction 0.75 vs 0.31), but not across the full trial period (0.61 vs 0.54).
INTERPRETATION: The trial suggests a modest reduction in relapse risk and short-term symptom improvement with MMB for Moms versus usual care. Strengths include pragmatic design and low attrition (77–78% follow-up). However, the effect on relapse is modest (HR ~0.74), the CI approaches 1, and symptom benefits did not persist postpartum. Funding from NIH/NIMH supports credibility, but generalisability to non-academic settings or outside the USA is uncertain.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: MMB for Moms may offer a non-pharmacological adjunct for perinatal relapse prevention, particularly during pregnancy, but the clinical impact appears limited and not sustained postpartum; integration should be cautious pending replication and cost-effectiveness data.

item.title: [15] Effects of EEG neurofeedback in adults with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder: a systematic review of randomised and non-randomised studies.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: This systematic review examined whether EEG neurofeedback improves symptoms, cognition, or brain activity in adults with ADHD, comparing standard and personalised training protocols. Seven studies (three RCTs, four non-randomised; n = 390) were included.
FINDINGS: RCTs showed small, generally non-significant effects on ADHD symptoms versus controls (effect sizes not reported). Non-randomised studies reported larger symptom reductions, but with high risk of bias. Cognitive gains were inconsistent and likely due to practice effects. Protocol-specific EEG changes were observed without convergence across studies. No treatment-related adverse events were reported.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited by small samples, heterogeneous protocols, variable controls, and risk of bias. RCTs do not currently support efficacy over placebo. Non-randomised studies suggest potential benefit but are prone to confounding. High-quality, blinded RCTs with standardised outcome measures are needed to determine clinical utility.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: EEG neurofeedback cannot be recommended as an evidence-based treatment for adult ADHD based on current data. Clinicians should discuss this uncertainty with patients and consider established treatments while awaiting better trials.

item.title: [12] Undertreatment of Wernicke encephalopathy in alcohol-related clinical contexts: a scoping review of diagnosis, thiamine regimens, and clinical management.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Wernicke encephalopathy (WE) is a preventable neurological emergency in alcohol use disorder (AUD) that is often missed or undertreated due to diagnostic uncertainty and heterogeneous management. This scoping review (PRISMA-ScR) mapped evidence on diagnosis and thiamine regimens in AUD or clinically significant alcohol use, focusing on practice variability and undertreatment.
FINDINGS: Only 26 studies were included, with only two RCTs on thiamine regimens; no consensus on optimal dosing emerged. Diagnostic criteria varied widely, and observational studies consistently reported undertreatment, including delayed initiation and frequent use of oral thiamine in high-risk scenarios. Protocolized, guideline-concordant care was associated with earlier parenteral thiamine use in suspected/confirmed WE.
INTERPRETATION: The evidence base is limited, heterogeneous, and underpowered, with no clear optimal thiamine regimen. While diagnostic variability and undertreatment are well-documented, the strength of conclusions is constrained by the lack of high-quality trials and inconsistent diagnostic criteria. Early recognition and parenteral thiamine in high-risk cases remain plausible but unproven strategies to reduce morbidity.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Clinicians should prioritize early suspicion of WE in AUD patients, use parenteral thiamine in high-risk cases, and follow local protocols where available, while acknowledging the lack of definitive evidence for optimal dosing or regimen.

item.title: [11] Protocol for a parallel-group superiority randomized controlled trial comparing Sage- a couple psychotherapy- to supportive individual psychotherapy for borderline personality disorder.
item.description:
BACKGROUND: Borderline personality disorder (BPD) carries high mortality and morbidity, and frontline treatments are often inaccessible or only partially effective. Sage is a novel, protocolized couple psychotherapy for BPD that targets both patient symptoms and relationship conflict, but its superiority over standard supportive care has not yet been tested in a rigorous trial. This is a single-blind, parallel-group RCT protocol comparing Sage to supportive individual psychotherapy in 152 couples where one partner has BPD.
FINDINGS: The trial randomizes couples to 16 weeks of Sage (couple-based) versus supportive individual psychotherapy (separate sessions for patient and partner). Primary outcome is BPD symptom change; secondary outcomes include relationship conflict and partner mental health. Assessments occur at baseline, mid-treatment, post-treatment, and 1-, 3-, and 6-month follow-ups. Primary analysis will use intent-to-treat generalized mixed linear models. No results are reported yet.
INTERPRETATION: This is a well-designed, adequately powered RCT with masked assessors and independent supervision to prevent drift, which strengthens internal validity. However, as a protocol paper, no outcome data are available, so efficacy, effect sizes, and safety remain unknown. The design addresses an important gap—testing whether adding a relationship-focused component improves outcomes—but generalizability may be limited by the requirement of a stable intimate partner and the exclusion of individuals without one.
CLINICAL RELEVANCE: Until results are published, clinicians should view Sage as an experimental intervention. Standard evidence-based treatments for BPD (e.g., DBT, MBT) remain first-line while this trial is ongoing.

item.title: [10] [Efficacy and tolerability of co-administration of clozapine with atypical antipsychotics in patients with treatment-resistant schizophrenia, comorbid with chemical addictions].
item.description:
BACKGROUND: The study compared six clozapine-plus-atypical-antipsychotic combinations in 470 adults with treatment-resistant paranoid schizophrenia, 83 % of whom also had a comorbid substance use disorder. It is a six-arm, open-label RCT conducted across multiple Russian psychiatric centres (2018–2026).
FINDINGS: After 42 days, combinations with cariprazine and, to a lesser extent, lurasidone produced significantly greater reductions in positive and negative symptoms than the other four regimens (p < 0.05). The cariprazine group also had the longest subsequent outpatient treatment duration. No adverse events were attributed to the combinations.
